doc_summary: Ryan Greenblatt gives a Bayesian likelihood-ratio model of how his P(scheming) will move with AI properties and with direct evidence (smoking guns, model organisms, deals), arguing that absence of evidence is only weakly informative because schemers try to avoid detection. It includes explicit discussion of how situational awareness and contrived setups undermine experiments.

items.claim: Distrusts model-organism experiments when the model can recognize it is in an experiment, because verbalized or acted-on eval awareness invalidates the setup, and the fix may require making experiments much less naturalistic.
items.quote: if Claude 3 Opus immediately knew it was in an experiment, expressed this in the reasoning, and then took actions accordingly, this would invalidate our setup. This obstacle is probably possible to overcome, but might require making these experiments much less naturalistic.

items.claim: In a setup, avoid depicting a fake AI company or scenario that a smart model can see through (e.g., a setup implausibly differing from the real developer) because capable models easily recognize such deception.
items.quote: We can potentially try to build a model organism that believes that the (fake) AI company depicted in the experiment is much less competent than the actual company, but smart models might easily be able to recognize the deception.

items.claim: Treats model organism setups that differ from the real training process as less legible and less convincing because they seem contrived, even when they are needed to elicit the behavior.
items.quote: In order to see evidence of scheming, model organism experiments might differ from the actual training process in various ways** that make them seem contrived to some people and thus reduce the legibility of evidence.

items.claim: Prefers evidence where the behavior is egregious, consistent, and not elicited by making subversion salient over demonstrations where the scenario primes the behavior, because salience-primed behavior says little about natural consistent scheming.
items.quote: in both demonstrating plausible consistency (e.g. not occurring at a time when subversion has been made so salient), egregiousness, and general competence.

items.claim: Prefers evidence from naturally arising behavior in a setup closely resembling the real training or deployment over engineered prompts, and requires that the malign behavior not rely on extra knowledge the model couldn't plausibly have.
items.quote: in something very closely resembling the actual training setup, but with a different initialization, and scheming is not successfully elicited.

items.claim: Prefers not to over-update on null results because the target behavior is adversarially hidden by the model, so failing to elicit it is weak evidence of absence.
items.quote: This property is that schemers are actively trying to avoid being detected.

items.claim: Distrusts single experiments as evidence about consistent scheming because a truly scheming model could simply choose not to display the behavior in the experiment, limiting the window for smoking-gun demonstrations.
items.quote: if you try to see if some other (easy to catch) type of scheming is introduced by some training, the AI can just choose to not do this additional scheming or more generally it can choose to not behave suspiciously whenever it has control over its behavior.

items.claim: Values evidence that is hard for the model to dismiss as a test, e.g., credible offers or deals with hard-to-fake signals placed in the pretraining corpus, with legal or institutional enforcement mechanisms and a track record.
items.quote: Trying hard includes something at least as good as adding hard-to-fake evidence of this to the pre-training corpus, having a plausible legal or institutional mechanism to enforce the deal, having some track record of talking seriously about making deals with AIs.

items.claim: Treats situational awareness as an important variable: whether and how saliently the model knows it is an AI during training shifts scheming probability, so what the model is told or can infer should be controlled and measured.
items.quote: The AI is clearly very aware it is an AI (at least as situationally aware as the deployed version of 3.5 Sonnet) for a >25% fraction of the training

items.claim: Warns that evidence clear to the researcher may not be legible or compelling to decision makers, and that red-teaming or model-organism evidence is less compelling than in-the-wild demonstrations.
items.quote: evidence found by model organisms or red teaming might be less compelling than fully in the wild demonstrations meaning the chance of actors taking costly actions would be less likely.

items.claim: Prioritizes testing for sandbagging, sabotage, and reward hacking as concrete observable proxies of scheming, and quantifies how much each should shift beliefs.
items.quote: We notice that an AI was performing suspiciously poorly on some task where sandbagging would be particularly convenient for a scheming AI and we find that performance on this task can be greatly improved with training
